outcomes.question: Our company year ended 30 June 2026. When is ECI due, and can we skip it if revenue was S$4.8 million but ECI is S$30,000?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ECI filing and waiver requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. For the stated FYE of 30/06/2026, the three-month ECI filing deadline is 30/09/2026, unless a filing exception applies. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.
- Official source: [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Whole-question gaps:**
- Issue plan: The reconciled issue plan does not establish coverage of the complete question.

sources.documentTitle: IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing
sources.sourceText:
ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.

If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS

If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

What is ECI

ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Learn about taxable income and tax-allowable expenses.

A company may receive up to $30,000 in CIT Rebate. The CIT Rebate applicable to the company for YA 2026 will be automatically computed in the company’s tax assessment based on the ECI/ Form C/ Form C-S/ Form C-S (Lite) filed by the company.

[UPDATED!] To provide further support for companies to manage their cashflow needs as they navigate the impact of the energy crisis, the CIT Rebate will be enhanced to 50% of the corporate tax payable for YA 2026.

Determining if Your Company Needs to File ECI

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless:

• Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or

• Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

ECI Filing Waiver

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met:

• Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and

• ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

1 Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver. If your company is new, learn when to file its first ECI.

Your company’s ECI filing status for the YA at mytax.iras.gov.sg may show 'Ready to File'.

For the financial year ending 30 Jun 2024:

Revenue  | ECI  | Does my company need to file ECI?

$5 million  | $100,000  | Yes

$10 million  | Nil  | Yes

•

•

• You do not need to file the ECI for your company if it is nil and your company's annual revenue is $5 million or below.

•

• If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI. You can fill in the ECI to be taxed at 17% as '0' in the digital service.

•

•

• If your company is required to file its ECI but fails to do so within 3 months from the end of its financial year, a Notice of Assessment may be issued based on an estimation of your company's income.

•

•

• I received a Notice of Assessment even though my company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver. What should I do?

•

•

• If your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver but is issued a Notice of Assessment, write in via myTax Mail before the payment due date to confirm that your company's annual revenue is $5 million or below and the ECI is nil for the said Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS will amend the assessment accordingly and no enforcement action will be taken for non-payment of the estimated taxes.

•

•

• Yes, IRAS sends a notification to companies before the end of their financial year on the need to file ECI. If your company assesses that it meets the conditions for the ECI filing waiver, it need not proceed with the filing.

•

FILE WITHIN 3 MONTHS FROM END OF FINANCIAL YEAR

Your company will receive a notification from IRAS to file its ECI in the last month of its financial year.

If your company did not receive the notification and does not satisfy the conditions to be exempted from ECI filing, it is still required to file within 3 months from the end of its financial year.

Examples of ECI Filing Due Dates Based on Different Financial Year Ends

Example 2: Determining the Date of 1st GIRO Deduction

Following Example 1 above, Company A files its ECI in Jan and 10 instalments are granted for the tax payable of $10,000.

Filing Date  | Between 1 and 20 Jan | Between 21 and 26 Jan

When filing the ECI, Company A can report its revenue as '$80,000' and the ECI figure as '$5,645' under the 17% tax rate category.

View more examples on how to calculate ECI (PDF, 186KB).

• For Tax Agents: User Guide - File Estimated Chargeable Income (PDF, 616KB)

Declaration of Revenue for ECI Filing

Your company's revenue must be declared when filing ECI.

Revenue is a company's main source of income and excludes items such as gain on disposal of fixed assets.

• If your company is an investment holding company, its main source of income is its investment income (e.g. interest and dividend income).

• Where the audited financial statements are not yet available, you may refer to the company’s management accounts for the purpose of declaring the revenue amount. If the actual revenue amount based on the audited financial statements differs from that declared during the ECI filing, but there is no change in your ECI, you do not need to revise the revenue amount.

issues.subject: ECI filing and waiver requirements

claims.text: ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.

If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

sources.sourceText:
WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment

For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Withholding Tax (WHT) Filing and Payment Due Date

Share:

•

•

•

•

•

•

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

•

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Scenarios | Date of payment to the non-resident  

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

sources.sourceText:
WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment

For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Withholding Tax (WHT) Filing and Payment Due Date

Share:

•

•

•

•

•

•

Payers must file and pay the WHT to IRAS by the due date.

WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).

On this page:

As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.

Learn more through our e-Learning video on the Filing and Payment of WHT.

If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.

Refer to your acknowledgement page for payment details after filing WHT.

Definition of date of payment

The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates:

For all payments except director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration).

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

For director’s fees

• When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios:

◦ Director's fees approved in arrears

For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM.

◦ Director's fees approved in advance

For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.

•

• When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident

• The date of actual payment

Scenarios | Date of payment to the non-resident  

Filing and payment due date

Technical assistance fees
A non-resident company issued an invoice dated 26 Mar 2025 to a payer for technical assistance fees in respect of services rendered. The invoice stated that the amount must be paid within 30 days.
The payer received the invoice on 30 Apr 2025 and paid the non-resident on 19 May 2025.  | 26 Mar 2025
(based on invoice date)  | 15 May 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 26 May 2025.

Royalty payment
The agreement stated that royalties at 5% of sales shall accrue to the non-resident at the end of each quarter.
In this instance, the royalty period from Apr to Jun 2025 was accrued on 30 Jun 2025 (end of quarter), and the royalty payment was made to the non-resident on 15 Jul 2025. | 30 Jun 2025
(based on date of accrual)  | 15 Aug 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Aug 2025.

Director’s fee
The director’s fee of $50,000 for the period from 01 Jan 2024 to 31 Dec 2024, was voted and approved in the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 2 Jul 2025.
However, the fee was only paid to the director on 29 Sep 2025.  | 2 Jul 2025
(based on AGM date)  | 15 Sep 2025

For GIRO payer, deduction takes place on 25 Sep 2025.

Multiple payments for a single engagement (non-resident professional or public entertainer)

If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Late payment penalty

Penalties will be imposed if the WHT is paid to IRAS after the payment due date or if the GIRO deduction is unsuccessful.

FAQs

Can I consolidate and file my WHT submission?

Yes, you can consolidate and file WHT twice a year, on 15 June and 15 December of each year if you are claiming tax exemption (i.e. tax rate is 0%) under the DTA and ARI.

For example:

Your WHT exempted (i.e. tax rate is 0%) payment to a non-resident is due every 15 of the month. Instead of filing for WHT monthly, you can consolidate and file 6 records on 15 June and the remaining 6 records on 15 December.

outcomes.question: We bought a delivery van for taxable business deliveries and a staff medical check-up in the same GST period. Are both input-tax claims allowed?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on staff medical expenses** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS states that staff medical input tax is generally disallowed under regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. Subject to the ordinary input-tax conditions, the stated exceptions are expenses obligatory under WICA or a qualifying Industrial Relations Act collective agreement; or, for expenses incurred on or after 1 October 2021, treatment connected with a work-related health risk or requirement and required under relevant Singapore written law. For the advisory limb, IRAS specifies treatment related to COVID-19 and required under a written advisory of the Government or a Singapore public authority. IRAS specifically says Primary Care Plan expenses do not meet the described work-related exception. A claim needs the expense date, legal/collective-agreement basis, work-related risk and mandate evidence, GST registration and invoice facts. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**GST input tax on a delivery van used for business deliveries** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS says input tax on other motor vehicles such as delivery vans is not blocked under the motor-car restriction, because those vehicles do not fall within the motor-car definition. A GST-registered business may claim input tax on the van purchase and running expenses only if the ordinary input-tax conditions are met; the vehicle classification and supporting claim facts still matter. sources.sourceText:
Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.

Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.

Yes, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car that is used by a third party, you will be allowed input tax claims on the cost and running expenses of the motor car incurred, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met

Input tax claims on motor car expenses for cars used by you or your employees are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations. Use of the motor car includes both: • physical use (e.g. motor car driven by your company staff or chauffeur to transport your company directors or business associates); and • economic use (i.e., use of the car to generate income or make supplies e.g. a consultancy firm uses its motor car to transport its preferred clients for a fee).

No, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car used by a person connected to you (e.g. your subsidiary), you cannot claim input tax on the cost and running expenses of the motor car, unless you satisfy both of the following conditions (in addition to the conditions for claiming input tax): 1. You recover the motor car expenses from the connected person. Where you recover only a portion of the motor car expenses incurred, you can only claim input tax to the extent of the portion recovered; and. 2. The recovery is not ancillary to any primary supply made by you to the connected person.

Yes, input tax claims are allowed on motor vehicles (e.g. lorry, van, motorcycle) that do not fall under the definition of a 'motor car'*, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met.

Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.

Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.

Yes, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car that is used by a third party, you will be allowed input tax claims on the cost and running expenses of the motor car incurred, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met

Input tax claims on motor car expenses for cars used by you or your employees are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations. Use of the motor car includes both: • physical use (e.g. motor car driven by your company staff or chauffeur to transport your company directors or business associates); and • economic use (i.e., use of the car to generate income or make supplies e.g. a consultancy firm uses its motor car to transport its preferred clients for a fee).

No, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car used by a person connected to you (e.g. your subsidiary), you cannot claim input tax on the cost and running expenses of the motor car, unless you satisfy both of the following conditions (in addition to the conditions for claiming input tax): 1. You recover the motor car expenses from the connected person. Where you recover only a portion of the motor car expenses incurred, you can only claim input tax to the extent of the portion recovered; and. 2. The recovery is not ancillary to any primary supply made by you to the connected person.

outcomes.question: We gave S$2,000 to an approved Singapore IPC in December 2026 and supplied our UEN. What corporate tax deduction is generally available, and until when does the enhanced deduction run under current guidance?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** Donations are non-deductible expenses in arriving at adjusted profit. For donations made from 1 January 2016 through 31 December 2029, a company may claim a deduction of 2.5 times the amount donated to an approved Institution of a Public Character (IPC) or the Singapore Government to benefit the local community. The company must provide its UEN to the approved IPC. IRAS says approved donation amounts are pre-filled in Form C-S, Form C-S (Lite) or Form C based on information obtained from IPCs. In the tax computation, add back all donations, then deduct 2.5 times approved donations; the deduction is on a preceding-financial-year basis. The 2.5-times deduction applies to donations made from 1 January 2016 through 31 December 2029 under the captured current guidance. The donee must be an approved IPC or the Singapore Government, and a Government donation must benefit the local community. For an IPC donation, the company must provide its UEN to the IPC to receive the deduction. Approved donations are considered on a preceding-financial-year basis. Donations outside the approved-donation category remain non-deductible business expenses under this cited rule. This record does not cover individual income-tax donations, other incentive schemes, tax-exemption computation, or whether a named donee is currently approved. For case-specific application, consider: Donation date and financial year. Donee identity and current approved-IPC status, or whether a Singapore Government donation benefits the local community. Donation amount and the amount recorded by IRAS; whether the company provided its UEN to the IPC. This guidance does not calculate the company’s adjusted profit, chargeable income or tax deduction amount. Confirm that the donee and donation are eligible and reconcile the amount with the applicable YA before filing. [IRAS | Tax Treatment of Business Expenses (A-F)](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/income-deductions-for-companies/business-expenses/tax-treatment-of-business-expenses-(a-f))

**Source:** IRAS | Tax Treatment of Business Expenses (A-F) (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations): Donations
Donations are non-deductible expenses as they are not incurred in the production of income.
However, for donations made from 1 Jan 2016 to 31 Dec 2029*, you can claim a tax deduction of 2.5 times the amount donated to an approved Institution of a Public Character (IPC) or the Singapore Government to benefit the local community
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations): Your company is required to provide its Unique Entity Number (UEN) to the approved IPC in order to be given a tax deduction on the approved donations.
To enhance your filing experience, the approved donation amounts will be pre-filled in the Form C-S/ Form C-S (Lite)/ Form C
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations): Step 1: Add back all donations made (approved donations or otherwise) to arrive at the adjusted profit as donations are non-deductible expenses.
Step 2: Claim a tax deduction of 2.5 times the amount of approved donations. You can check the amount of approved donations made by the company via the View Donations digital service at mytax.iras.gov.sg. Tax deduction on approved donations is allowable on a preceding financial year basis
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations): Tax deduction on approved donations is allowable on a preceding financial year basis.

outcomes.question: Our company incurred a book loss this year but has S$800,000 of revenue. Must we file ECI?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ECI filing and waiver requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.
- Official source: [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Whole-question gaps:**
- Issue plan: The reconciled issue plan does not establish coverage of the complete question.

Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.

If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

sources.sourceText:
ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. sources.documentTitle: IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing
sources.sourceText:
ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.

If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS

If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing

Share:

What is ECI

ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).

Learn about taxable income and tax-allowable expenses.

A company may receive up to $30,000 in CIT Rebate. The CIT Rebate applicable to the company for YA 2026 will be automatically computed in the company’s tax assessment based on the ECI/ Form C/ Form C-S/ Form C-S (Lite) filed by the company.

[UPDATED!] To provide further support for companies to manage their cashflow needs as they navigate the impact of the energy crisis, the CIT Rebate will be enhanced to 50% of the corporate tax payable for YA 2026.

ECI Filing Waiver

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met:

• Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and

•

•

• If your company is required to file its ECI but fails to do so within 3 months from the end of its financial year, a Notice of Assessment may be issued based on an estimation of your company's income.

•

• Find out more about the estimated Notice of Assessment.

•

•

• I received a Notice of Assessment even though my company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver. What should I do?

•

•

• If your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver but is issued a Notice of Assessment, write in via myTax Mail before the payment due date to confirm that your company's annual revenue is $5 million or below and the ECI is nil for the said Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS will amend the assessment accordingly and no enforcement action will be taken for non-payment of the estimated taxes.

•

•

2.

Example

This is Company A’s Profit and Loss statement for the financial year 2024 (Year of Assessment (YA) 2025):

Profit and Loss statement  | $

FAQs

•

• How do I file the ECI if my company has changed its financial year and the change is across Years of Assessment (YA)?

•

•

• Yes, you can still file the ECI if a Notice of Assessment for the Year of Assessment (YA) has not been issued to your company. However, your company will not be granted instalments for the payment of the estimated taxes.

You will receive a consolidated acknowledgement statement for all the clients that you file for in a single submission. The Notices of Assessment will be issued directly to your clients.

•

Paying Estimated Tax

You can view your company’s Notice of Assessment at mytax.iras.gov.sg after IRAS has processed its ECI filing. The Notice of Assessment is an official Notice that states the amount of tax to be paid.

No Notice of Assessment will be issued if your company files nil for ECI.

When to Pay Estimated Tax

Your company needs to pay the tax payable amount within 1 month from the date of the Notice of Assessment, unless it qualifies to pay via instalments.

Difference in ECI Amount Declared and Chargeable Income Reported in Form C-S/ Form C-S (Lite)/ Form C

Less than ECI amount declared earlier  | Excess tax paid earlier will be refunded automatically.

More than ECI amount declared earlier  | Pay the additional tax within 1 month from the date of the Notice of Assessment.

Note: If there is a significant difference between the ECI declared earlier and the chargeable income reported in the Form C-S/ Form C-S (Lite)/ Form C subsequently, your company may be required to provide an explanation to IRAS.

The GIRO arrangement must be approved before the payment due date (i.e. 1 month from the date of the Notice of Assessment) for your company to qualify to pay via instalments.

•

• If the GIRO arrangement is not approved before the payment due date, your company will have to pay the full amount of estimated tax within 1 month from the date of the Notice of Assessment.

•

How to Revise ECI

Go to the Revise/ Object to Assessment digital service at mytax.iras.gov.sg to file the revised ECI amount.

For assistance on revising ECI, refer to these guides:

• For Tax Agents: User Guide - Revise/ Object to Assessment (PDF, 3.3MB)

Late Filing/ Failure to File ECI

Estimated Notice of Assessment

If your company is late in filing or fails to file its ECI, an estimated Notice of Assessment may be issued based on your company’s past years’ income or other information available to IRAS.

Your company has to pay the full tax amount within 1 month from the date of the Notice of Assessment. It will not enjoy instalment payment.

Payment must be made based on the estimated Notice of Assessment even if your company has filed an objection. If the assessment is subsequently revised, any excess payment will be refunded to your company.

Objection to Estimated Assessment

If your company disagrees with the estimated tax assessment, an objection must be filed within 2 months from the date of the Notice of Assessment.

When filing the objection, your company has to provide the reasons for the late filing or failure to file ECI and the revised ECI amount.

outcomes.question: We paid a non-resident company for remote software support carried out wholly overseas. Does Singapore WHT apply?
outcomes.answer:
The available verified evidence does not cover the full tax question. I cannot establish the tax treatment from it.

Information still needed to complete the question:
- Whether the overseas recipient is the beneficial owner of the payment
- Whether treaty relief is available and the residence/beneficial-owner documents supporting it
- Payment or deemed-payment date

Admitted source evidence and reviewed summaries:

Withholding tax on royalties, technical services and management fees paid to non-residents depends on the nature of the rights or services, where services are physically performed, recipient residence, treaty position and payment date. Services performed in Singapore can attract non-final withholding at the prevailing corporate income tax rate.

Reviewed local editorial summary (nonverbatim; Income Tax Act 1947); [related IRAS guidance page](<https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/payments-to-non-resident-company/payments-that-are-subject-to-withholding-tax>); recorded scope 2026-01-01 to open-ended.

> Whether the DTA provides relief from double taxation of payments for technical services depends on the tax treatment of such services as provided for in the DTA. Generally, the payments are subject to withholding tax if the non-resident company has a permanent establishment in Singapore. The concept of permanent establishment is used in a DTA between 2 Contracting States to determine whether a person resident in a Contracting State has a taxable/ business presence in another Contracting State.

[IRAS | Payments that are subject to withholding tax](<https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/payments-to-non-resident-company/payments-that-are-subject-to-withholding-tax>) — retrieved official evidence.

> the Singapore-Malaysia DTA), the tax to be withheld depends on the tax rate stated in this Article. However, if the non-resident company has a permanent establishment in Singapore, the provisions of the Business Profits Article apply instead.

> Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

[IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](<https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing>) — retrieved official evidence.

> Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

[IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](<https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing>) — retrieved official evidence.

> Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

[IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](<https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing>) — retrieved official evidence.

This evidence states the recorded rules; it does not by itself confirm that every condition is met in this case.

outcomes.question: An employee has S$9,200 monthly OW in 2026. What OW base is subject to CPF before applying the employee's rate?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF contribution rates by age group** (party in scope: Employee)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. For monthly wages above S$750, the employer/employee rates are: age 55 and below 17%/20%; above 55 to 60, 16%/18%; above 60 to 65, 12.5%/12.5%; above 65 to 70, 9%/7.5%; above 70, 7.5%/5%. For an actual payroll case, identify the year, birth date, citizenship/PR conversion date and any approved PR-rate election before selecting a table. New age-group rates start on the first day of the month after the 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday. Do not apply this 2026 table to another payroll year. [CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/content/dam/web/employer/employer-obligations/documents/CPFcontributionratesfrom1Jan2026.pdf)

**Source:** CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026 (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF contribution rates by age group): Table 1

Notes:
For Private Sector / Non-Pensionable Employees (Ministries, Statutory Bodies & Aided Schools)
OW: Ordinary Wages (capped at OW ceiling of $8,000)
AW: Additional Wages
TW: Total Wages = OW + AW
Max: Maximum contribution on OW
Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share
4) If there is only OW payable for the month, the maximum contribution on OW is to be rounded to the nearest dollar for the total CPF contributions and rounded down
to the nearest dollar for employee’s share of CPF contributions. If there are OW and AW payable for the same month, compute and sum up the CPF contributions
that are payable for OW and AW and apply the rounding rules accordingly.
5) To compute CPF contributions, use the CPF contribution calculator (cpf.gov.sg/employer > Tools and services > Calculators > CPF contribution calculator).
These rates are also applicable to 1st and 2nd year Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) employees and their employers after CPF Board approves their joint application
to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.

outcomes.question: We paid a S$12,000 bonus in February 2026. How do we determine the CPF-able AW ceiling for this employee?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence incomplete

**CPF additional wage ceiling and year-end recalculation** (party in scope: Employer)
- **Evidence gap:** Verified quotations do not support the requested topic cpf-bonus-backpay.
- **Evidence gap:** CPF additional wage ceiling and year-end recalculation: Verified quotations do not support the requested topic cpf-bonus-backpay.

**Source:** Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF additional wage ceiling and year-end recalculation): Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF contribution rates by age group** (party in scope: Employee)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. For monthly wages above S$750, the employer/employee rates are: age 55 and below 17%/20%; above 55 to 60, 16%/18%; above 60 to 65, 12.5%/12.5%; above 65 to 70, 9%/7.5%; above 70, 7.5%/5%. For an actual payroll case, identify the year, birth date, citizenship/PR conversion date and any approved PR-rate election before selecting a table. New age-group rates start on the first day of the month after the 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday. Do not apply this 2026 table to another payroll year. [CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/content/dam/web/employer/employer-obligations/documents/CPFcontributionratesfrom1Jan2026.pdf)

**Source:** CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026 (live external)

Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share
4) If there is only OW payable for the month, the maximum contribution on OW is to be rounded to the nearest dollar for the total CPF contributions and rounded down
to the nearest dollar for employee’s share of CPF contributions. If there are OW and AW payable for the same month, compute and sum up the CPF contributions
that are payable for OW and AW and apply the rounding rules accordingly.

to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Determine your employees’ CPF contributions

> $750
* Max. of $1,000 | * Max. of $400
Notes:
For Private Sector / Non-Pensionable Employees (Ministries, Statutory Bodies & Aided Schools)
OW: Ordinary Wages (capped at OW ceiling of $8,000)
AW: Additional Wages
TW: Total Wages = OW + AW
Max: Maximum contribution on OW
Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share
4) If there is only OW payable for the month, the maximum contribution on OW is to be rounded to the nearest dollar for the total CPF contributions and rounded down
to the nearest dollar for employee’s share of CPF contributions. If there are OW and AW payable for the same month, compute and sum up the CPF contributions
that are payable for OW and AW and apply the rounding rules accordingly.
5) To compute CPF contributions, use the CPF contribution calculator (cpf.gov.sg/employer > Tools and services > Calculators > CPF contribution calculator).
These rates are also applicable to 1st and 2nd year Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) employees and their employers after CPF Board approves their joint application
to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share

5) To compute CPF contributions, use the CPF contribution calculator (cpf.gov.sg/employer > Tools and services > Calculators > CPF contribution calculator).

to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.
