outcomes.question: We paid the CPF contribution on an Additional Wage that is now above the AW ceiling. Should we wait for the year-end automatic refund?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for the issues identified below; other issues remain incomplete.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence incomplete

**CPF employer refund timing and application requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **Evidence gap:** Verified quotations do not support the requested topic cpf-additional-wages.

**CPF employer refund timing and application requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** Refund requests for CPF contributions generally must be made immediately and no later than one year from payment; the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field identifies the payment date. For conditional wages, the one-year period instead runs from when the wages are due to be repaid to the employer, as stated in employment terms or a mutual agreement, and that date must be entered in the application. Before applying, the employer must return the employee share directly to the employee. CPF Board effects refunds only to the extent of funds available in the employee’s CPF account. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions should be claimed promptly; excess CPF Annual Limit contributions paid from 2023 are automatically refunded to the employer’s Direct Debit Account from February 2024. The general and entire-submission application deadline is one year from contribution payment, using the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” record field. Conditional-wage refunds use the repayment due date, not the contribution payment date. The employer must first return the employee share where applicable; refunds depend on funds available in employee CPF accounts. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions are a prompt-application category. CPF Annual Limit excess contributions paid from 2023 are refunded automatically to the employer from February 2024; this is distinct from an application for an AW-ceiling refund. For case-specific application, consider: Refund category and CPF payment date. For conditional wages, the contractual or mutually agreed repayment due date. Whether the employee share was returned and funds remain available in CPF account(s). For AW or annual-limit excess, the relevant year and excess category. Do not infer a refund deadline when the payment date, conditional-wage repayment date or calendar anniversary is unclear. The source does not establish that a particular refund application will be accepted or the amount CPF Board will refund. [CPFB | Applying for refund of CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/compliance-and-rectifications/applying-for-refund-of-cpf-contributions)
- **Evidence gap:** CPF employer refund timing and application requirements: Verified quotations do not support the requested topic cpf-additional-wages.

**Source:** Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.
- Official source: [Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/069IW00000KUuZCYA1)

**Source:** CPFB | Applying for refund of CPF contributions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date of payment of the CPF contributions. You can refer to the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field in your record of payment to determine the date of payment.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid on conditional wages must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date wages are supposed to be repaid to the employer. This will be the date stated in the terms of employment or based on mutual agreement
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): You’re responsible to refund the employee’s share of CPF contributions (where applicable) directly to your employee before submitting the application.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund is subject to availability of funds
We’ll effect the refund based on the available funds in the employee’s CPF account
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund of payments made in excess of Additional Wage ceiling
Once you have discovered that you paid CPF contributions in excess of the AW ceiling for any of your employees, you should apply for a refund of the CPF contributions made promptly.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF employer refund timing and application requirements): Refund of contributions paid in excess of CPF Annual Limit
From February 2024, any CPF contributions paid in excess of the CPF Annual Limit will be refunded automatically to the employer's Direct Debit Account maintained with CPF Board. This applies to excess contributions paid from year 2023
- Official source: [CPFB | Applying for refund of CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/compliance-and-rectifications/applying-for-refund-of-cpf-contributions)

- Issue plan: The reconciled issue plan does not establish coverage of the complete question.
- CPF employer refund timing and application requirements: Verified quotations do not support the requested topic cpf-additional-wages.

sources.sourceText:
Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date of payment of the CPF contributions. You can refer to the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field in your record of payment to determine the date of payment.

Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid on conditional wages must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date wages are supposed to be repaid to the employer. This will be the date stated in the terms of employment or based on mutual agreement

You’re responsible to refund the employee’s share of CPF contributions (where applicable) directly to your employee before submitting the application.

Refund is subject to availability of funds
We’ll effect the refund based on the available funds in the employee’s CPF account

Refund of payments made in excess of Additional Wage ceiling
Once you have discovered that you paid CPF contributions in excess of the AW ceiling for any of your employees, you should apply for a refund of the CPF contributions made promptly.

Refund of contributions paid in excess of CPF Annual Limit
From February 2024, any CPF contributions paid in excess of the CPF Annual Limit will be refunded automatically to the employer's Direct Debit Account maintained with CPF Board. This applies to excess contributions paid from year 2023

Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date of payment of the CPF contributions. You can refer to the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field in your record of payment to determine the date of payment.

Any request for refund of CPF contributions paid on conditional wages must be made immediately and no later than one year from the date wages are supposed to be repaid to the employer. This will be the date stated in the terms of employment or based on mutual agreement

You’re responsible to refund the employee’s share of CPF contributions (where applicable) directly to your employee before submitting the application.

Refund is subject to availability of funds
We’ll effect the refund based on the available funds in the employee’s CPF account

Refund of payments made in excess of Additional Wage ceiling
Once you have discovered that you paid CPF contributions in excess of the AW ceiling for any of your employees, you should apply for a refund of the CPF contributions made promptly.

Refund of contributions paid in excess of CPF Annual Limit
From February 2024, any CPF contributions paid in excess of the CPF Annual Limit will be refunded automatically to the employer's Direct Debit Account maintained with CPF Board. This applies to excess contributions paid from year 2023

issues.subject: CPF employer refund timing and application requirements

claims.text:
Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF contribution rates by age group** (party in scope: Employee)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s 2026 contribution table applies from 1 January 2026 to Singapore Citizens or third-year-onward SPRs in private-sector or non-pensionable public-service employment. For monthly wages above S$750, the employer/employee rates are: age 55 and below 17%/20%; above 55 to 60, 16%/18%; above 60 to 65, 12.5%/12.5%; above 65 to 70, 9%/7.5%; above 70, 7.5%/5%. For an actual payroll case, identify the year, birth date, citizenship/PR conversion date and any approved PR-rate election before selecting a table. New age-group rates start on the first day of the month after the 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday. Do not apply this 2026 table to another payroll year. [CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/content/dam/web/employer/employer-obligations/documents/CPFcontributionratesfrom1Jan2026.pdf)

**Source:** CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026 (live external)

Steps to compute CPF contribution:
1) Compute the total CPF contribution (rounded to the nearest dollar), i.e., to be rounded down for an amount less than 50 cents and rounded up for an amount of 50
cents and above.
2) Compute the employee’s share of CPF contribution (rounded down to the nearest dollar).
3) Employer’s share = Total contribution - Employee’s share
4) If there is only OW payable for the month, the maximum contribution on OW is to be rounded to the nearest dollar for the total CPF contributions and rounded down
to the nearest dollar for employee’s share of CPF contributions. If there are OW and AW payable for the same month, compute and sum up the CPF contributions
that are payable for OW and AW and apply the rounding rules accordingly.

These rates are also applicable to 1st and 2nd year Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) employees and their employers after CPF Board approves their joint application
to contribute to CPF at full employer- full employee rates.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

outcomes.question: We dismissed an employee for misconduct, but payroll cannot release final salary on that day. How soon must we pay, and when is a payslip due?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence incomplete

**MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements** (party in scope: Employer)

- **Evidence gap:** MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements: Verified quotations do not support the requested topic mom-salary-payment.

**Source:** Itemised pay slips (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): From 1 April 2016, all employers must issue itemised pay slips to employees covered by the Employment Act.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): Employers must issue itemised pay slips to all employees covered by the Employment Act.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): Pay slips must include the items below, unless an item is not applicable. For example, if overtime pay does not apply to you, your pay slip need not include items 9 to 11.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): Give together with payment to employee.

• If unable to give together, to be given within three working days of payment.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): In the case of termination or dismissal, must give pay slip together with outstanding salary.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): Format | Soft or hard copy (including handwritten)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): If payments are made more than once a month, employers can consolidate pay slips. The consolidated pay slip must contain details of all payments made since the last pay slip.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): items to include, when and how to give them.

Employers must issue itemised pay slips to all employees covered by the Employment Act.

When

• Give together with payment to employee.

• If unable to give together, to be given within three working days of payment.

• In the case of termination or dismissal, must give pay slip together with outstanding salary.

Format | Soft or hard copy (including handwritten).

Pay slips must include the items below, unless an item is not applicable. For example, if overtime pay does not apply to you, your pay slip need not include items 9 to 11. If payments are made more than once a month, employers can consolidate pay slips. The consolidated pay slip must contain details of all payments made since the last pay slip.

Number | Item description

1 | Full name of employer.

2 | Full name of employee.

3 | Date of payment (or dates, if the pay slips consolidates multiple payments).

4

Basic salary

For hourly, daily or piece-rated workers, indicate all of the following:

• Basic rate of pay, e.g. $X per hour.

• Total number of hours or days worked or pieces produced.

5 | Start and end date of salary period.

6

Allowances paid for salary period, such as:

• All fixed allowances, e.g. transport.

• All ad-hoc allowances, e.g. one-off uniform allowance.

7

Any other additional payment for each salary period, such as:

• Bonuses

• Rest day pay

• Public holiday pay

8

Deductions made for each salary period, such as:

• All fixed deductions (e.g. employee’s CPF contribution).

• All ad-hoc deductions (e.g. deductions for no-pay leave, absence from work).

9 | Overtime hours worked.

10 | Overtime pay.

11 | Start and end date of overtime payment period (if different from item 5 start and end date of salary period).

12 | Net salary paid in total.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements): Employers must keep a record of all pay slips issued.

Format | Soft or hard copy, including handwritten.

For how long?

• For current employees: Latest two years.

• For ex-employees: Last two years, to be kept for one year after the employee leaves employment.
- Official source: [Itemised pay slips](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/itemised-payslips)

- Issue plan: The reconciled issue plan does not establish coverage of the complete question.

outcomes.question: Our employee is still on probation at five completed months. Can we deny paid annual leave until confirmation?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Paid Annual Leave** (party in scope: Not established)

**Source:** MOM | Annual leave eligibility and entitlement (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): Annual leave eligibility and entitlement
If you are covered by the Employment Act and have worked for at least 3 months, you are entitled to annual leave.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): Eligibility
You are entitled to paid annual leave if you have worked for your employer for at least 3 months.
You can only apply for annual leave after working for 3 months.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): Entitlement
Your annual leave entitlement depends on how many years of service you have with your employer. Your year of service begins from the day you start work with your employer.
Year of service | Days of leave
1st | 7
2nd | 8
3rd | 9
4th | 10
5th | 11
6th | 12
7th | 13
8th and thereafter | 14
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): How pro-rated annual leave is calculated
Annual leave is pro-rated using this formula: (Number of completed months of service ÷ 12 months) × Number of days of annual leave entitlement.
If the fraction of a day is less than one-half, round it down.
If it is half or more, round it up to one day.
The period from 14 to 31 July is disregarded as it is not a completed month.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): If you are taking unpaid leave
You should exclude periods of approved unpaid leave when calculating your annual leave entitlement.
If you have taken unpaid leave, your employer can pro-rate your leave entitlement based on how many complete months you have worked.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Paid Annual Leave): If you are serving notice
If you have resigned, your notice period is included when calculating your pro-rated annual leave.
- Official source: [MOM | Annual leave eligibility and entitlement](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/leave/annual-leave/eligibility-and-entitlement)

sources.sourceText:
Annual leave eligibility and entitlement
If you are covered by the Employment Act and have worked for at least 3 months, you are entitled to annual leave.

Eligibility
You are entitled to paid annual leave if you have worked for your employer for at least 3 months.
You can only apply for annual leave after working for 3 months.

Entitlement
Your annual leave entitlement depends on how many years of service you have with your employer. Your year of service begins from the day you start work with your employer.
Year of service | Days of leave
1st | 7
2nd | 8
3rd | 9
4th | 10
5th | 11
6th | 12
7th | 13
8th and thereafter | 14

Pro-rated leave
3 to 12 months | Based on the number of completed months you have worked. This applies even if you’re still on probation.
More than a year | Based on the number of completed months you worked in your current year.

How pro-rated annual leave is calculated
Annual leave is pro-rated using this formula: (Number of completed months of service ÷ 12 months) × Number of days of annual leave entitlement.
If the fraction of a day is less than one-half, round it down.
If it is half or more, round it up to one day.
The period from 14 to 31 July is disregarded as it is not a completed month.

If you are taking unpaid leave
You should exclude periods of approved unpaid leave when calculating your annual leave entitlement.
If you have taken unpaid leave, your employer can pro-rate your leave entitlement based on how many complete months you have worked.

If you are serving notice
If you have resigned, your notice period is included when calculating your pro-rated annual leave.

sources.sourceText:
Annual leave eligibility and entitlement
If you are covered by the Employment Act and have worked for at least 3 months, you are entitled to annual leave.

Eligibility
You are entitled to paid annual leave if you have worked for your employer for at least 3 months.
You can only apply for annual leave after working for 3 months.

Entitlement
Your annual leave entitlement depends on how many years of service you have with your employer. Your year of service begins from the day you start work with your employer.
Year of service | Days of leave
1st | 7
2nd | 8
3rd | 9
4th | 10
5th | 11
6th | 12
7th | 13
8th and thereafter | 14

Pro-rated leave
3 to 12 months | Based on the number of completed months you have worked. This applies even if you’re still on probation.
More than a year | Based on the number of completed months you worked in your current year.

How pro-rated annual leave is calculated
Annual leave is pro-rated using this formula: (Number of completed months of service ÷ 12 months) × Number of days of annual leave entitlement.
If the fraction of a day is less than one-half, round it down.
If it is half or more, round it up to one day.
The period from 14 to 31 July is disregarded as it is not a completed month.

If you are taking unpaid leave
You should exclude periods of approved unpaid leave when calculating your annual leave entitlement.
If you have taken unpaid leave, your employer can pro-rate your leave entitlement based on how many complete months you have worked.

If you are serving notice
If you have resigned, your notice period is included when calculating your pro-rated annual leave.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee has 11 paid public holidays each year. If a holiday falls on the rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday; if it falls on a non-working day, another day off or an extra day at the gross rate is due. Working on a public holiday ordinarily earns holiday gross pay plus an additional day at the basic rate; overtime applies beyond normal hours. By mutual agreement, the day may be substituted. Part IV coverage limits which employees may use time off in lieu. Distinguish a holiday on a working day, non-working day, or rest day. For holiday gross pay, the employee must not be absent without consent or reasonable excuse on the working day immediately before or after the holiday; authorised leave on either day is permitted. No holiday pay is due when the holiday itself falls during approved unpaid leave. Additional basic-rate pay is the default for working on the holiday; substitute-holiday arrangements require mutual agreement. An employee outside Employment Act coverage is governed by the contract. Time off in lieu of hours worked is available only to employees not covered by Part IV under the stated arrangement. Rest-day pay and any excess-hours overtime are separate entitlements. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act and Part IV coverage. Work schedule and whether the date is a working, non-working or rest day. Whether the employee worked, hours worked, agreed substitution/time-off arrangements, and relevant absence or unpaid-leave facts. Does not decide a specific date’s gazetted holiday status or compute holiday pay without schedule and wage facts. Does not replace separate rest-day, overtime or part-time rules. **Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)

You are entitled to 11 paid public holidays a year in accordance with the Employment Act. If you are required to work on a public holiday, your employer should pay you an extra day’s salary or grant you off in lieu.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): The 11 public holidays
If you are covered by the Employment Act, you are entitled to 11 paid public holidays in a year.
The 11 gazetted public holidays are:
New Year’s Day
Chinese New Year – first day
Chinese New Year – second day
Hari Raya Puasa
Hari Raya Haji
Good Friday
Labour Day

National Day
Deepavali
Christmas Day
If the holiday falls on a rest day, the next working day will be a paid holiday.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): Holiday pay
You are entitled to your gross rate of pay on a public holiday, if:
You were not absent on the working day immediately before or after a holiday without consent or a reasonable excuse.
You are on authorised leave (e.g. sick leave, annual leave, unpaid leave) on the day immediately before or after a holiday.
You are not entitled to holiday pay if the holiday falls on your approved unpaid leave.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): Public holidays falling on a rest day or non-working day
In accordance with the Employment Act, if a public holiday falls on a non-working day, you are entitled to another day off or one extra day's salary in lieu of the public holiday at the gross rate of pay.
If a public holiday falls on your rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday.
If you are on a 5-day work week, Saturday would be considered your non-working day and Sunday would be your rest day.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): If you work on a public holiday
If you work on a public holiday, by default, your employer should pay you an additional day's pay.
Alternatively, by mutual agreement, you can get one of the following:
A public holiday in lieu.
Time off in lieu (only for employees not covered under Part 4 of Employment Act).
If you are required to work on a public holiday, you should be paid an extra day’s salary at the basic rate of pay.
Your monthly gross salary already includes payment for the holiday, so your employer need only pay you an additional day’s pay.
If you work on a public holiday that falls on:
A working day:
An extra day’s salary at the basic rate of pay.
The gross rate of pay for that holiday.
Overtime pay if you work beyond your normal hours of work.
A non-working day (e.g. Saturday for employees on a 5-day work week):
Overtime pay for extra hours worked on a Saturday.
One extra day’s salary at the gross rate of pay or another day off for the public holiday.
A rest day:
Payment for work done on a rest day.
Overtime pay if you work beyond your normal hours of work.
The next working day will be a paid holiday instead.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): Public holiday in lieu
If you work on a public holiday, you and your employer can mutually agree to substitute a public holiday for another working day.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Public holiday entitlement and pay): Time off in lieu for employees not covered under Part 4 of Employment Act
If you are not covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act, your employer can grant you time off in lieu for working on a public holiday. The time off should consist of a mutually agreed number of hours.
If there is no mutual agreement on the duration of time off in lieu, your employer can decide on one of the following:
Pay an extra day’s salary at the basic rate of pay for one day’s work.
For working 4 hours or less on a holiday, grant time off in lieu of 4 hours on a working day.
For working more than 4 hours on a holiday, grant a full day off on a working day.

**Source:** Salary Deductions | Ministry of Manpower (MOM) (offline fixture title) (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM employer salary deduction authorization, purpose and limits): For employees covered by the Employment Act, salary deductions are permitted only on specified grounds. Deductions for damage or loss require the employer to establish the employee’s direct fault and give the employee an opportunity to explain; that deduction is limited to 25% of one month’s salary on one occasion. Normal authorised deductions are generally capped at half of salary for a salary period; exceptions include absence, loan or advance repayment, overpayment recovery and cooperative payments. Authorised final-payment deductions may exceed the normal cap. Employee consent is not universal permission to deduct, and foreign-worker levy recovery is not permitted.

outcomes.question: We gave a soft-copy payslip three days after paying salary. Is electronic format allowed and is the timing acceptable?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM itemised payslip content, delivery format and retention requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **MOM rule explanation:** Employers must issue itemised pay slips to employees covered by the Employment Act together with payment. If that is not possible, the pay slip must be given within three working days of payment. For termination or dismissal, it must be given together with outstanding salary. MOM allows a soft or hard copy, including handwritten. The pay slip must include the employer and employee names, payment date, basic salary, salary period, applicable allowances, other payments, deductions and total net salary; overtime hours, pay and period are included where applicable. If payments are made more than once a month, pay slips may be consolidated, but the consolidated slip must show all payments since the last slip. Employers must retain issued pay slips: the latest two years for current employees, and the last two years for ex-employees for one year after they leave. The requirements apply to employees covered by the Employment Act. Only applicable pay slip items need to be shown; overtime items 9 to 11 need not be included when overtime pay does not apply. The fallback is three working days after payment only when the employer cannot give the pay slip with payment. Consolidation is permitted for multiple monthly payments, but must include every payment since the previous slip. Items that do not apply need not be shown; MOM’s page gives overtime items as an example. This rule does not calculate final-salary deadlines or determine Employment Act coverage for a particular worker. For case-specific application, consider: Employment Act coverage. Salary period, payment date and pay components applicable to the employee. Whether pay slips are consolidated, whether overtime applies, current or former employee status, and the employee’s departure date if applicable. Three working days are not converted into calendar days. The captured page does not establish current coverage of a particular worker or calculate a case-specific final salary. [Itemised pay slips](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/itemised-payslips)

Employers must issue itemised pay slips to all employees covered by the Employment Act.

When

• Give together with payment to employee.

• If unable to give together, to be given within three working days of payment.

• In the case of termination or dismissal, must give pay slip together with outstanding salary.

Format | Soft or hard copy (including handwritten).

Pay slips must include the items below, unless an item is not applicable. For example, if overtime pay does not apply to you, your pay slip need not include items 9 to 11. If payments are made more than once a month, employers can consolidate pay slips. The consolidated pay slip must contain details of all payments made since the last pay slip.

Number | Item description

1 | Full name of employer.

2 | Full name of employee.

3 | Date of payment (or dates, if the pay slips consolidates multiple payments).

4

Basic salary

For hourly, daily or piece-rated workers, indicate all of the following:

• Basic rate of pay, e.g. $X per hour.

• Total number of hours or days worked or pieces produced.

5 | Start and end date of salary period.

6

Allowances paid for salary period, such as:

• All fixed allowances, e.g. transport.

• All ad-hoc allowances, e.g. one-off uniform allowance.

7

Any other additional payment for each salary period, such as:

• Bonuses

• Rest day pay

• Public holiday pay

8

Deductions made for each salary period, such as:

• All fixed deductions (e.g. employee’s CPF contribution).

• All ad-hoc deductions (e.g. deductions for no-pay leave, absence from work).

9 | Overtime hours worked.

10 | Overtime pay.

11 | Start and end date of overtime payment period (if different from item 5 start and end date of salary period).

12 | Net salary paid in total.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MOM itemised payslip content, delivery format and retention requirements): Employers must keep a record of all pay slips issued.

Format | Soft or hard copy, including handwritten.

For how long?

• For current employees: Latest two years.

• For ex-employees: Last two years, to be kept for one year after the employee leaves employment.

Format | Soft or hard copy (including handwritten)

outcomes.question: Our local company changed its registered office on 20 October 2026. Can we wait until the annual return to update ACRA?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA company entity information update requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says registered entities must notify it of changes within 14 days from the date of change; foreign companies have 30 days. The listed details include the entity email address and registered office address. The time limit runs from the change, so the annual return is not a substitute for making a required update within that period. The 14-day period applies to registered entities except foreign companies, for which the page gives 30 days. The source lists entity name, email address, business activities, registered office and other entity information; the steps vary by information category. The page distinguishes foreign companies and does not establish every filing duty for officers, share capital, annual returns, VCCs or historical periods. For case-specific application, consider: Entity type and the category of information changed. The date of the change and any category-specific filing facts. A calendar deadline requires a confirmed change date and entity category. For an entity-specific answer, confirm the applicable filing route. [Updating an entity’s information | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/resources/guides-forms/updating-entitys-information/)

sources.documentTitle: ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs)
sources.sourceText:
All Singapore companies must hold AGMs each year unless they:

Are exempt from holding an AGM

Choose to dispense with the AGM

Your due date for holding an AGM is based on your:

Company's financial year end (FYE)

Company type (listed or non-listed company)

AGM deadlines: FY ending on or after 31 August 2018

Company type

Due date

Listed companies

Within four months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within six months after FYE

Note: You must hold AGMs on time to avoid penalties.

When you can skip holding an AGM

Private companies can skip holding an AGM if they are exempt or choose to dispense with an AGM.

Exemptions from holding an AGM

Private companies do not need to hold an AGM if they meet any of these criteria:

Send financial statements to all members within five months after the FYE.

Dormant, not listed (or not a subsidiary of a listed company), and has total assets of $500,000 or less (consolidated value if it is an ultimate parent).

Dispensing with AGMs

Private companies can:

Choose not to hold AGMs if all members pass a resolution to dispense with the AGM.

Handle AGM matters through written resolutions instead.

Examples include hard copies, emails, or legible formats agreed by the company and members. Contact a professional or lawyer if you need help with resolution formats.

You may include the written resolution when you file your annual return.

Note: You must declare your AGM details when you file an annual return. This applies whether you held an AGM, were exempt or dispensed with holding an AGM.

When members can still request AGMs

Even if your company is exempt or has dispensed with AGMs, members can still request one:

Safeguards for requesting AGMs

Situation

Details

A member wants an AGM

When they can request: Up to 14 days before the sixth month deadline. This deadline is six months after the FYE.

What you must do: Hold an AGM within six months after the FYE.

You may apply for an extension of time before this deadline, if needed.

A member or auditor wants an AGM after receiving financial statements

When they can request: Within 14 days of receiving financial statements

What you must do: Hold a general meeting within 14 days of the request.

sources.documentTitle: ACRA | Deadline & requirements for annual returns
sources.sourceText:
An annual return is an online form you have to file with ACRA.

It contains key details about your company, such as:

Company name and registration number

Company type, business activities, and registered office address

Details of directors, the company secretary, and members

Share information and financial statements (if required)

This information helps stakeholders (like investors and partners) to make informed decisions.

Annual filing requirements

Company officers must file annual returns on time to avoid enforcement action.

Company requirements

Filing requirement

Details

Annual return filing with ACRA

All companies registered in Singapore must file an annual return with ACRA each year. This applies as long as your company is listed as “live” with us.

You must file an annual return even if your company is:

Inactive or dormant

Granted a tax waiver by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)

Filing your annual return keeps your company’s public information accurate. As a director, it is your legal duty to file on time.

Tax filing with IRAS

After filing your annual return, you must still file your taxes with IRAS. Check IRAS filing due dates and guides (opens in new tab).

Note: Dormant companies must also file tax returns unless IRAS has granted a waiver. Learn more about filing requirements for dormant companies (opens in new tab).

When to file your annual returns

Your deadline for filing the Annual Return is based on:

Your company's FYE

Your company type (listed or non-listed company)

Filing deadlines

Company type

Filing deadline

Listed companies

Within five months after FYE

Listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within six months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within seven months after FYE

Non-listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within eight months after FYE

Note: You must file your annual returns on time to avoid penalties. You cannot change your FYE after the filing deadline has passed.

**ACRA company secretary appointment and sole-director requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s guide says every company must have a company secretary, appointed within six months of successful registration, and the position cannot remain vacant for more than six months. sources.documentTitle: ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs)
sources.sourceText:
All Singapore companies must hold AGMs each year unless they:

Are exempt from holding an AGM

Choose to dispense with the AGM

Your due date for holding an AGM is based on your:

Company's financial year end (FYE)

Company type (listed or non-listed company)

AGM deadlines: FY ending on or after 31 August 2018

Company type

Due date

Listed companies

Within four months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within six months after FYE

Note: You must hold AGMs on time to avoid penalties.

When you can skip holding an AGM

Private companies can skip holding an AGM if they are exempt or choose to dispense with an AGM.

Exemptions from holding an AGM

Private companies do not need to hold an AGM if they meet any of these criteria:

Send financial statements to all members within five months after the FYE.

Dormant, not listed (or not a subsidiary of a listed company), and has total assets of $500,000 or less (consolidated value if it is an ultimate parent).

Dispensing with AGMs

Private companies can:

Choose not to hold AGMs if all members pass a resolution to dispense with the AGM.

Handle AGM matters through written resolutions instead.

Examples include hard copies, emails, or legible formats agreed by the company and members. Contact a professional or lawyer if you need help with resolution formats.

You may include the written resolution when you file your annual return.

Note: You must declare your AGM details when you file an annual return. This applies whether you held an AGM, were exempt or dispensed with holding an AGM.

When members can still request AGMs

Even if your company is exempt or has dispensed with AGMs, members can still request one:

Safeguards for requesting AGMs

Situation

Details

A member wants an AGM

When they can request: Up to 14 days before the sixth month deadline. This deadline is six months after the FYE.

What you must do: Hold an AGM within six months after the FYE.

You may apply for an extension of time before this deadline, if needed.

A member or auditor wants an AGM after receiving financial statements

When they can request: Within 14 days of receiving financial statements

What you must do: Hold a general meeting within 14 days of the request.

An annual return is an online form you have to file with ACRA.

It contains key details about your company, such as:

Company name and registration number

Company type, business activities, and registered office address

Details of directors, the company secretary, and members

Share information and financial statements (if required)

This information helps stakeholders (like investors and partners) to make informed decisions.

Annual filing requirements

Company officers must file annual returns on time to avoid enforcement action.

Company requirements

Filing requirement

Details

Annual return filing with ACRA

All companies registered in Singapore must file an annual return with ACRA each year. This applies as long as your company is listed as “live” with us.

You must file an annual return even if your company is:

Inactive or dormant

Granted a tax waiver by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)

Filing your annual return keeps your company’s public information accurate. As a director, it is your legal duty to file on time.

Tax filing with IRAS

After filing your annual return, you must still file your taxes with IRAS. Check IRAS filing due dates and guides (opens in new tab).

Note: Dormant companies must also file tax returns unless IRAS has granted a waiver. Learn more about filing requirements for dormant companies (opens in new tab).

When to file your annual returns

Your deadline for filing the Annual Return is based on:

Your company's FYE

Your company type (listed or non-listed company)

Filing deadlines

Company type

Filing deadline

Listed companies

Within five months after FYE

Listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within six months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within seven months after FYE

Non-listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within eight months after FYE

Note: You must file your annual returns on time to avoid penalties. You cannot change your FYE after the filing deadline has passed.

Note: You must declare your AGM details when you file an annual return. This applies whether you held an AGM, were exempt or dispensed with holding an AGM.

When members can still request AGMs

Even if your company is exempt or has dispensed with AGMs, members can still request one:

Safeguards for requesting AGMs

Situation

Details

A member wants an AGM

When they can request: Up to 14 days before the sixth month deadline. This deadline is six months after the FYE.

What you must do: Hold an AGM within six months after the FYE.

You may apply for an extension of time before this deadline, if needed.

A member or auditor wants an AGM after receiving financial statements

When they can request: Within 14 days of receiving financial statements

What you must do: Hold a general meeting within 14 days of the request.

sources.sourceText:
An annual return is an online form you have to file with ACRA.

It contains key details about your company, such as:

Company name and registration number

Company type, business activities, and registered office address

Details of directors, the company secretary, and members

Share information and financial statements (if required)

This information helps stakeholders (like investors and partners) to make informed decisions.

Annual filing requirements

Company officers must file annual returns on time to avoid enforcement action.

Company requirements

Filing requirement

Details

Annual return filing with ACRA

All companies registered in Singapore must file an annual return with ACRA each year. This applies as long as your company is listed as “live” with us.

You must file an annual return even if your company is:

Inactive or dormant

Granted a tax waiver by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)

Filing your annual return keeps your company’s public information accurate. As a director, it is your legal duty to file on time.

Tax filing with IRAS

After filing your annual return, you must still file your taxes with IRAS. Check IRAS filing due dates and guides (opens in new tab).

Note: Dormant companies must also file tax returns unless IRAS has granted a waiver. Learn more about filing requirements for dormant companies (opens in new tab).

When to file your annual returns

Your deadline for filing the Annual Return is based on:

Your company's FYE

Your company type (listed or non-listed company)

Filing deadlines

Company type

Filing deadline

Listed companies

Within five months after FYE

Listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within six months after FYE

Non-listed companies

Within seven months after FYE

Non-listed companies with:

A share capital

An overseas branch register

Within eight months after FYE

Note: You must file your annual returns on time to avoid penalties. You cannot change your FYE after the filing deadline has passed.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA financial statement preparation and filing exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. A solvent exempt private company may qualify not to file; dormant-relevant-company relief requires all Companies Act section 201A conditions. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. sources.documentTitle: Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title)
sources.sourceText:
If your company wishes to conduct fund management activities regulated under the Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA) , it must apply to be a licensed fund management company (LFMC) that holds a capital markets services (CMS) licence.

If your company solely manages venture capital funds, it may apply to be an LFMC that operates under the simplified venture capital fund manager (VCFM) regime.

Individuals performing key functions in a fund management company, such as portfolio construction and allocation, research and advisory, business development and marketing or client servicing are required to be representatives.

You can find out more about fund management activity and the differences between an LFMC and VCFM here.

When we assess your company to be an LFMC or VCFM, MAS considers factors such as:

• Credibility and substantiveness of the business model and plan, and the associated risks;

• Effectiveness of risk management and compliance controls;

• Fund management track record and expertise of an LFMC applicant's management, parent company and major shareholders;

• Fitness and propriety of the applicant, its shareholders and directors; and

• Ability to meet the relevant minimum financial requirements prescribed under the SFA.

In addition, your company needs to operate from a dedicated and secure office space that is accessible only by your company’s directors and staff.

For more information on the admission criteria and applicable requirements, please refer to the Guidelines on Licensing and Conduct of Business for Fund Management Companies.

VCFMs are subject to a simplified set of admission criteria – please refer to Appendix 4 of the aforementioned guidelines.

If your company is able to operate under an existing class exemption, it does not require a licence. Examples of companies that may be eligible for exemption include those that:

• Manage assets for related corporations or related family members;

• Manage a pool of immovable assets for accredited and institutional investors; or

• Manage a pool of non-capital markets products for accredited and institutional investors.

You can find more information on exemptions under section 99 of the SFA and paragraph 5 of the Second Schedule to the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations .

sources.documentTitle: Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title)
sources.sourceText:
If your company wishes to conduct fund management activities regulated under the Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA) , it must apply to be a licensed fund management company (LFMC) that holds a capital markets services (CMS) licence.

If your company solely manages venture capital funds, it may apply to be an LFMC that operates under the simplified venture capital fund manager (VCFM) regime.

Individuals performing key functions in a fund management company, such as portfolio construction and allocation, research and advisory, business development and marketing or client servicing are required to be representatives.

You can find out more about fund management activity and the differences between an LFMC and VCFM here.

When we assess your company to be an LFMC or VCFM, MAS considers factors such as:

• Credibility and substantiveness of the business model and plan, and the associated risks;

• Effectiveness of risk management and compliance controls;

• Fund management track record and expertise of an LFMC applicant's management, parent company and major shareholders;

• Fitness and propriety of the applicant, its shareholders and directors; and

• Ability to meet the relevant minimum financial requirements prescribed under the SFA.

In addition, your company needs to operate from a dedicated and secure office space that is accessible only by your company’s directors and staff.

For more information on the admission criteria and applicable requirements, please refer to the Guidelines on Licensing and Conduct of Business for Fund Management Companies.

VCFMs are subject to a simplified set of admission criteria – please refer to Appendix 4 of the aforementioned guidelines.

If your company is able to operate under an existing class exemption, it does not require a licence. Examples of companies that may be eligible for exemption include those that:

• Manage assets for related corporations or related family members;

• Manage a pool of immovable assets for accredited and institutional investors; or

• Manage a pool of non-capital markets products for accredited and institutional investors.

You can find more information on exemptions under section 99 of the SFA and paragraph 5 of the Second Schedule to the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations .

outcomes.question: Our VCFM has not confirmed its financial year-end. Can we use the nil-misconduct date to set Form 25A and treat it as satisfying all fund returns?
outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for the issues identified below; other issues remain incomplete.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Venture Capital Fund Manager** (party in scope: Not established)

**MAS VCFM annual declaration and Form 25A reporting requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s current VCFM compliance toolkit says a venture capital fund manager must submit Form 25A, an annual declaration of changes to key appointments, assets under management, investor types and numbers, fund types, and deals, within one month after its financial year end. The toolkit cites Regulation 14(6) of the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations. The due date for a specific manager depends on its financial year end. [VENTURE CAPITAL FUND MANAGERS](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit--vcfms29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

**MAS VCFM nil misconduct return requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS FAQ 13 says that financial institutions covered by SFA 04-N11 are not required to submit a nil misconduct declaration for the calendar year ending 31 December 2026, notwithstanding the existing Notice wording. The Misconduct Reporting Notices effective 1 January 2027 also do not require nil declarations. If you mean a different reporting year, identify that calendar year: this FAQ passage does not establish its deadline. [FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (“FAQs”) ON](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas/regulations-and-financial-stability/regulations-guidance-and-licensing/financial-advisers/faq/faqs-on-misconduct-reporting-notices-under-the-faa-ia-and-sfa.pdf)

**MAS VCFM toolkit scope and fund-level requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS describes the VCFM toolkit as a reference for common applications, forms and submissions under the Securities and Futures Act. MAS says it is not exhaustive and expressly excludes reporting obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Therefore, Form 25A does not establish that every reporting obligation of each managed fund is complete. Identify applicable fund-level requirements separately for each fund and relevant activity; this source does not provide a complete fund-level checklist. [VENTURE CAPITAL FUND MANAGERS](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit--vcfms29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

**Source:** Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title) (live external)

sources.documentTitle: Fund Management Licensing | Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) (offline fixture title)
sources.sourceText:
If your company wishes to conduct fund management activities regulated under the Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA) , it must apply to be a licensed fund management company (LFMC) that holds a capital markets services (CMS) licence.

If your company solely manages venture capital funds, it may apply to be an LFMC that operates under the simplified venture capital fund manager (VCFM) regime.

Individuals performing key functions in a fund management company, such as portfolio construction and allocation, research and advisory, business development and marketing or client servicing are required to be representatives.

You can find out more about fund management activity and the differences between an LFMC and VCFM here.

When we assess your company to be an LFMC or VCFM, MAS considers factors such as:

• Credibility and substantiveness of the business model and plan, and the associated risks;

• Effectiveness of risk management and compliance controls;

• Fund management track record and expertise of an LFMC applicant's management, parent company and major shareholders;

• Fitness and propriety of the applicant, its shareholders and directors; and

• Ability to meet the relevant minimum financial requirements prescribed under the SFA.

In addition, your company needs to operate from a dedicated and secure office space that is accessible only by your company’s directors and staff.

For more information on the admission criteria and applicable requirements, please refer to the Guidelines on Licensing and Conduct of Business for Fund Management Companies.

VCFMs are subject to a simplified set of admission criteria – please refer to Appendix 4 of the aforementioned guidelines.

If your company is able to operate under an existing class exemption, it does not require a licence. Examples of companies that may be eligible for exemption include those that:

• Manage assets for related corporations or related family members;

• Manage a pool of immovable assets for accredited and institutional investors; or

• Manage a pool of non-capital markets products for accredited and institutional investors.

You can find more information on exemptions under section 99 of the SFA and paragraph 5 of the Second Schedule to the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations .
